title: CAT Sample Paper Book: What to Look For and How to Actually Use It
meta_title: CAT Sample Paper Book: Pick It, Use It Right
meta_desc: What a good CAT sample paper book must contain and how to build a mock-then-analyse prep plan around it across VARC, DILR and Quant, with a free quiz.
excerpt: Most aspirants buy a CAT sample paper book, solve a few sets, feel busy, and learn nothing. The book is only as good as the routine you build around it. Here is what to look for and how to use it.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
A CAT aspirant I mentored last year had solved eleven sample papers by August and was still stuck at the 82nd percentile in her mocks. Eleven papers, no movement. The problem was not the papers — it was that she treated each one as a task to finish rather than a signal to read. That is the trap almost every candidate falls into, and it is exactly why choosing the right CAT sample paper book matters far less than knowing how to use one.

This post is about the book as a structured practice tool: what separates a genuinely useful one from a bundle of loose questions, and how to fold it into a prep timeline so that every paper you solve buys you a real percentile gain. If you just want a broad look at past papers, that is a different question. Here we are building a study plan around the book.

What a good CAT sample paper book must contain

The CAT is three sections — VARC, DILR and Quantitative Ability — sat under a strict per-section clock. A sample paper book that ignores that structure is a workbook, not a mock. Before you buy anything, check for these:

  • Full-length, sectionally-timed sets — 22–24 questions per section in the three-section pattern, not a random 100-question dump.
  • Worked solutions, not just an answer key. The whole value of a sample paper is in the why. A book that gives you only ‘Ans: C’ teaches you nothing about the shorter method you missed.
  • A realistic difficulty spread. Real CAT sections mix sitters, medium questions and two or three brutal ones designed to eat your clock. A book where every question is solvable in ninety seconds gives you false confidence.
  • The non-MCQ (TITA) format included — type-in-the-answer questions with no negative marking are a permanent feature, and your selection strategy for them is different.
  • An honest marking scheme — +3 per correct answer, −1 for a wrong MCQ, no penalty on TITA — so your practice score means something.

If a book gives you all five, the brand on the cover barely matters. What you do next matters far more.

Mock-then-analyse: the only discipline that works

Here is the rule I make every serious aspirant follow: the analysis takes longer than the paper. A CAT slot is two hours. Your review of it should run two to three. If you are spending twenty minutes checking answers and moving on, you are collecting papers, not improving.

How to run one paper properly

Solve it in one sitting under the exact clock — 40 minutes a section, no pausing, no phone. Then, before you look at a single solution, go back over your own attempt and mark each question honestly:

  • Got it right, quickly and confidently.
  • Got it right, but it took too long.
  • Got it wrong.
  • Left it — and note why you skipped.

Only then open the solutions. The gold is in categories two and four: the questions you could have banked but did not, and the ones you avoided out of fear rather than genuine difficulty. Keep an error log — a plain notebook column of the concept behind every miss. After four or five papers, patterns jump out. Maybe it is always Data Interpretation tables, or always Reading Comprehension inference questions. That log tells you what to fix; the raw score never does.

Fitting the book into a CAT timeline

Sample papers are a diagnostic and a rehearsal, not a way to learn concepts from scratch. Using them too early just tells you what you already know — that you are not ready. A workable sequence for a candidate starting six months out:

PhaseMonths to CATHow to use the book
Foundation6–4Concepts + topic drills. Solve papers section-wise, untimed, to spot weak areas.
Build-up4–2One full timed paper a week. Full analysis. Rework your error log.
Peak2–0Two timed papers a week, same time of day as your slot. Refine selection, not new theory.

Notice that the number of papers goes up as the exam nears, not the number of new topics. The last eight weeks are about temperament and question selection, and a sample paper book is the cheapest way to rehearse both.

Balancing VARC, DILR and Quant

Most aspirants over-practise the section they already like. If you love algebra, you will happily grind Quant and quietly dodge Verbal. The book cannot fix that bias — you have to. A rough weekly split I recommend: give the section you fear the most an extra 30 to 40 percent of your practice time.

DILR deserves a special note. It is the section that decides most calls in recent years, and it is the least about knowledge and the most about set selection — deciding in the first two minutes which of the four sets to attack and which to abandon. Use your sample papers specifically to practise walking away from a bad set. That single skill has rescued more scores than any formula.

A quick word on TITA and negative marking

Because TITA questions carry no penalty, your strategy there is the reverse of MCQs: attempt anything you can even partially crack. On MCQs, a wild guess at +3 against −1 is usually a bad bet unless you have eliminated two options. Practise this arithmetic of risk on paper long before slot day.

Try the quick quiz below

Below is a short, free eight-question CAT-quant quiz — the kind of arithmetic, algebra and DI reasoning a sample paper leans on. Attempt each under a rough two-minute clock, then read the explanations for anything you miss and add it to your error log. quiz.title: CAT Quant Warm-Up Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight CAT-level questions across arithmetic, algebra, numbers and data interpretation. Give yourself about two minutes each, pick an answer, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: CAT Quantitative Ability and DI fundamentals

questions.q: A shopkeeper marks goods 40% above cost and gives a 25% discount. His profit percent is:
questions.explanation: Let cost be 100. Marked price 140; after 25% discount the selling price is 105. Profit is 5 on 100, so 5%.
Square both sides: x^2 + 2 + 1/x^2 = 25, so x^2 + 1/x^2 = 23.

questions.q: Two pipes fill a tank in 12 and 18 minutes. Working together they fill it in:
questions.explanation: Combined rate is 1/12 + 1/18 = 5/36 per minute, so time is 36/5 = 7.2 minutes.

questions.q: A train 150 m long passes a pole in 15 seconds. Its speed is:
questions.explanation: Speed is 150/15 = 10 m/s. Multiply by 18/5 to get 36 km/h.

questions.q: The average of five consecutive even numbers is 24. The largest is:
questions.explanation: The middle number is the average, 24, so the numbers are 20, 22, 24, 26, 28. The largest is 28.

questions.q: In how many ways can the letters of the word LEVEL be arranged?
questions.explanation: LEVEL has 5 letters with L and E each repeated twice: 5!/(2!x2!) = 120/4 = 30.

questions.q: A sum doubles in 8 years at simple interest. In how many years will it triple?
questions.explanation: Doubling means interest equals the principal in 8 years, so the rate gives 100% in 8 years, i.e. 12.5% per year. Tripling needs 200% interest, which takes 16 years.

questions.q: If 30% of a number is 45, then 80% of the same number is:
questions.explanation: The number is 45/0.30 = 150. Then 80% of 150 is 120.

faq.q: Is a CAT sample paper book still useful when free mocks exist online?
faq.a: Yes, as a complement. A book gives you distraction-free, offline practice and, in a good one, cleaner worked solutions than many free platforms. The ideal setup is online mocks for the on-screen timing experience plus a sample paper book for focused, annotated review you can scribble on.

faq.q: How many CAT sample papers should I actually solve?
faq.a: Quality over quantity — 12 to 15 papers, each fully analysed, beats 30 half-reviewed ones. If your analysis is not taking longer than the paper itself, you are solving too many and learning too little.

faq.q: When in my preparation should I start solving full sample papers?
faq.a: Begin section-wise and untimed once your concepts are roughly in place, usually around three to four months out. Move to full, strictly-timed papers in the final eight to ten weeks, increasing frequency as the exam nears.

faq.q: Should I attempt every question in a CAT sample paper?
faq.a: No. CAT rewards selection. Practise identifying and skipping the two or three time-sinks per section, especially in DILR where walking away from a bad set is a core skill. On TITA questions, though, attempt freely since there is no negative marking.
